findings.description: The inline policy grants full wildcard actions on four major services (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) against Resource "*", which is effectively administrative control over compute, storage, and serverless resources in the account. Combined with the long-lived access key on the same user, a leaked credential yields total data access and the ability to launch or destroy infrastructure.

A permanent IAM access key is created for a human-style IAM user instead of using identity federation or an assumable role with temporary credentials. The key never expires and persists until manually rotated, and it inherits the near-administrative permissions of the attached inline policy.

No pgp_key is supplied, so the generated secret access key is written in cleartext into the Terraform state file (and encrypted_secret is never populated). Anyone with read access to the state backend obtains working credentials with ec2/s3/lambda/cloudwatch wildcard permissions.

The access key secret is surfaced through the output "secret", which is not marked sensitive. The value is printed on apply and readable via `terraform output`, widening the audience for the credential to anyone able to run plan/apply or read CI logs.

Permissions are granted through an inline user policy rather than a group or an assumable role, and no permissions boundary is set on the user. There is no guardrail limiting the maximum privilege the identity can hold, and because s3:* and lambda:* include policy- and function-modifying actions, this forms a privilege escalation path.
